Title: August 17, 2023 - Regular Boulder City Council Meeting
Overview: The council accepted the clean 2022 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report, heard extensive public comment on minimum wage and other issues, and approved the consent agenda. It placed a 50/50 split of the 0.15 percent sales tax renewal (Ordinance 8591) on the November ballot after defeating the 100 percent arts measure, then adopted Ordinance 8585 to raise the citywide occupancy limit for unrelated persons from three to five after a long public hearing.

Topic1.Title: Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (2022 audit)
Topic1.Summary: Audit subcommittee member David Gross presented the 2022 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and the audit by Clifton Larson Allen. The auditor issued a clean opinion with no significant deficiencies or material weaknesses, the 33rd consecutive year of the GFOA certificate of achievement. Council members thanked the audit committee and finance staff, and the council later approved the report on the consent agenda.

Topic2.Title: Open comment: minimum wage and public testimony
Topic2.Summary: Many residents, union members, and labor advocates urged the council to raise the local minimum wage to 15 dollars or more immediately rather than waiting until 2025. Speakers also raised concerns about airport noise, Human Services funding, the 0.15 percent sales tax, and a proposed mental health center. Staff committed to follow up on local business wage data and confirmed the city is still enforcing the camping ban.

Topic3.Title: Council questions on the 0.15 percent sales tax ballot options
Topic3.Summary: Council asked staff whether the existing 0.15 percent tax is dedicated to any purpose and whether a 50/50 compromise measure must be placed on the ballot if the council does not act. Deputy City Attorney Aaron Poe confirmed the petitioners' 100 percent arts measure would proceed to the ballot unless withdrawn. Council also discussed Human Services funding concerns and the timing of the ballot deadline.

Topic4.Title: Consent agenda and staff overview of ballot ordinances
Topic4.Summary: Council approved consent agenda items 3A through 3I unanimously after Councilmember Benjamin pulled item 3J for separate discussion. Item 3H was an annexation for which a council member disclosed prior work with the property owners but still considered themselves impartial. Deputy City Attorney Aaron Poe then summarized the status of the five ballot measure ordinances, including the staff-recommended changes to the 50/50 compromise ordinance 8591.

Topic5.Title: Budget impacts and votes on 0.15 percent sales tax ballot measures
Topic5.Summary: Budget Officer Mark Wolfe explained that the 2024 recommended budget was built assuming renewal of the 0.15 percent tax, and that a half-dedicated option still avoids service cuts while a full general fund option offers the most flexibility. Council adopted ordinance 8586 and ordinance 8587 unanimously and defeated ordinance 8588, which would dedicate 100 percent to arts, by a vote of five to two to four. Council then approved the 50/50 compromise ordinance 8591 by a vote of six to three.

Topic6.Title: Call-up check-in: vacation of utility easement at 2950 Hawthorne Avenue
Topic6.Summary: Staff presented a request to vacate a 14-foot-wide utility easement at 2950 Hawthorne Avenue, formerly 3320 28th Street, under case ADR 2023-00109. No council member asked to call up the item, so it proceeded without further review.

Topic7.Title: Occupancy limits: staff presentation on Ordinance 8585
Topic7.Summary: Planning staff presented Ordinance 8585, which would raise the citywide limit for unrelated occupants from three to five and change the limit for efficiency units to three. Staff described the project history, national comparisons, and community engagement results, including the 2,000 BeHeardBoulder responses that favored four more than five. The presentation also covered a proposed freeze on occupancy increases in non-conforming uses, with an option to limit it to university-adjacent zones, and the Planning Board's 4-3 recommendation of approval.

Topic8.Title: Occupancy limits: public hearing testimony
Topic8.Summary: Dozens of residents, students, co-op members, and housing advocates spoke in favor of raising the occupancy limit, citing affordability, chosen families, and the need for shared housing. Opponents, including many Martin Acres and Hill residents, raised concerns about noise, parking, trash, enforcement, the 2021 bedrooms-for-people vote, and the lack of rent guarantees. Several speakers also asked for affordability requirements, stronger code enforcement, and attention to climate and traffic impacts.

Topic9.Title: Council deliberation and adoption of Ordinance 8585
Topic9.Summary: Councilmember Rachel Friend moved to adopt Ordinance 8585, and a motion to remove the non-conforming use and occupancy provisions failed three to six. Council members who supported the change argued it would expand housing options, support students and chosen families, and that enforcement should target behaviors rather than people. Opponents said the change lacks affordability guarantees, overrides the 2021 vote, and could worsen neighborhood impacts, and the council then adopted Ordinance 8585 by a vote of six to three.
